Dear diary,
Today in PE Simran Ma'am said, "Hop to it!" so I hopped. Everyone laughed. I did not know why.
At lunch the girls played a game with a rope and said I was out. I don't know how I was out. I asked twice and Riddhi rolled her eyes.
The bell is SO loud. By the last period my head felt like it was full of bees.
After school Simran Ma'am called me and said, "Bhavna, 'hop to it' means hurry. I should have been clearer." She wrote it in my notebook. Now I have a page called Funny Sayings.
At home I lay under the dining table for a long time. Mumma let me.

qa.a: She took responsibility for being unclear, explained the phrase kindly and wrote it in Bhavna's notebook instead of scolding.

passage: Looking back at ninth grade, I can see how hard I worked just to seem normal. I studied the way Arohi laughed at lunch and copied the timing. Then I'd get home and could not speak at all. I'd lie on the floor of my room in the dark, and sometimes I cried for no reason I could name. My mother would put a glass of water by the door and say, "No questions today, Joseph." That door was the first place I could stop acting. I think it saved that whole year.

passage:
Friday night.
Class party today. I had my lines ready: "Nice shirt." "Haha, true." I copied Tejas every time he laughed, a half-second late. I kept my face moving. Nobody noticed anything. I think I did it perfectly.
In the auto home my hands started shaking. At home I couldn't answer when Papa asked about dinner. I went into my room and sat inside the cupboard with the door half shut. Everything was too loud, even the fan.
Papa didn't push. He left a cup of tea on the desk and said through the door, "I'm just outside if you want." That's all.

Saurabh

passage: In my first year of college I fixed old radios in my hostel room every evening, seven to ten, headphones on. People called me strange. A week later she knocked on my door holding a broken valve radio. "Fine, Jeevan. Prove it." We spent four hours on it. It crackled into life at midnight, playing old film songs. Now the radio club meets in my room, and Urmila tells new members, "Jeevan will tell you the truth, and he'll be right." I still keep my evenings quiet.

passage:
Subject: Working in the way I work best
Dear Pradeep,
Thank you for the first three weeks. I want to be honest about what helps me do my best work.
The open floor is very loud for me. By afternoon I find it hard to think. Could I sit at the desk near the back wall, or wear noise-cancelling headphones?
Spoken instructions in stand-ups slip away from me. If tasks could be written in the tracker, I will finish them faster and with fewer questions.
I sometimes skip the team lunch. It is not because I don't like the team; small talk tires me out.
I really enjoy the data cleaning project. I'd like to keep it.
Best,
Kiran

qa.q: What project does Kiran enjoy?
qa.a: Kiran enjoys the data cleaning project.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel on the open floor by the afternoon?
qa.a: Kiran feels drained and finds it hard to think, because the open floor is very loud.

qa.q: Why is Kiran's email a sensible way to ask for help?

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Kiran after reading the email?
qa.a: Pradeep may see Kiran as a committed colleague who knows how to work best, and realise the team lunch absence is not unfriendliness.

grounding: Shows a young adult who finds open offices, small talk and unclear instructions draining but works well with clear written tasks, and reasonably asks for adjustments.

passage: So you asked how the new job is going. Honestly? The first month I came home and lay on the floor every night. The office is one big hall, people chat by the kettle, and my manager, Francis, would say things like "just make it pop." I had no idea what that meant. I thought I was failing. Then I told him, "I'm autistic, and I work best with written steps." I was shaking when I said it. He just nodded and said, "Okay, what would help?" Now every task comes in a list with a deadline. I have a desk by the window. I'm Jasleen, and for the first time at work I feel understood. It's such a relief.

qa.q: What did Francis say when Jasleen explained how she works best?
qa.a: He nodded and said, "Okay, what would help?"

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Francis responded kindly?
qa.a: She felt relieved and understood, after being scared enough to shake while telling him.

qa.q: What made the adjustment easy once Jasleen spoke up?
qa.a: Francis asked what would help, then gave written task lists with deadlines and a quieter desk by the window.

qa.q: What would change if Francis had kept giving vague instructions like "make it pop"?
qa.a: Jasleen might have kept feeling like she was failing and coming home exhausted, and the team would lose her real strengths.

grounding: Shows an autistic adult drained by an open office and vague instructions, who asks for reasonable adjustments and feels relief at being understood.

passage:

Week six: Briefs now come on a shared page. Pooja sits in the small room by the plants. Harish just says "Morning" and moves on. She finished the brochure layout two days early, and Harish told the client, "Pooja's work is always exact." She went home and cooked dinner, humming.

passage: "Pooja beti, you think reading is easy for everyone? Let me tell you about a boy in Lucknow. Me. When I was nine, the letters jumped about like crickets. I hid my Urdu reader under the charpai and told my teacher the goat ate it. Everyone laughed, and I began to believe I was a duffer. But Master Hamid noticed that I could add sums in my head faster than anyone. He kept me back and said, 'A mind that fast is not stupid. We will read one page a day, slowly.' Every afternoon, one page. It took two years. Now look, I run the accounts for the whole market. So, your spelling test, na? We'll do it slowly." Wasim uncle folded his newspaper and opened her book.

qa.q: Where did Wasim hide his Urdu reader as a boy?
qa.a: He hid it under the charpai and told his teacher the goat ate it.

qa.q: How did young Wasim feel about himself before Master Hamid stepped in?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and began to believe he was a duffer, because the letters kept jumping and everyone laughed.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for young Wasim?
qa.a: Master Hamid noticed his quick mental sums, told him he was not stupid and read one page a day with him patiently.

qa.q: How might Master Hamid have seen young Wasim?
qa.a: Master Hamid saw a bright boy whose mind was fast and whose only difficulty was reading, not a lazy or stupid child.

grounding: An elder recalls being a bright child who stumbled over letters, hid books and thought he was stupid, until patient early help protected his confidence.

passage: Hafsa, nine, heard the substitute teacher say, "Everyone will read one paragraph aloud before the bell." Only ten minutes left. Her stomach dropped. The words on page forty were long and slippery; "was" kept looking like "saw." When her turn was three children away, she pushed her book into her bag and whispered, "I forgot it." At break she told her friend, "I'm stupid, that's why." Kunal Sir, the class teacher, had seen the book slide into the bag. He called Hafsa over at lunch. "You explained the water cycle better than anyone yesterday. Reading is hard work for you, not thinking." He phoned her Ammi that evening, and the next week Hafsa started reading sessions with the school's special teacher.

qa.q: What word kept looking like "saw" to Hafsa?
qa.a: The word "was" kept looking like "saw."

qa.q: How was Hafsa feeling as her turn to read came closer?
qa.a: She felt frightened and ashamed, so she hid her book and said she forgot it rather than read in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Kunal Sir do that protected Hafsa's confidence?
qa.a: He told her she thinks well and only reading is hard, then called her Ammi the same evening so she could start extra reading help.

qa.q: If you were Hafsa's friend at break, how might you see her comment?
qa.a: You might feel sad and surprised to hear her call herself stupid, because she seems clever to you.

grounding: Shows a bright child who stumbles over words and letters, hides her book and thinks she is stupid, protected by early help and patience.

passage: In their Jaipur flat, Seema's brother Yash found three storybooks stuffed under her mattress. "Why are these here?" he laughed. Seema, eight, snatched them. "Because I hate them." At school that day she had written "bog" for "dog" and "dab" for "bad," and the class had giggled. Yet at dinner she explained exactly why the building's water tank overflowed and how to fix the float. Yash stopped laughing. "You're smarter than me at this stuff." Seema stared at her plate. "Then why can't I read?" The next day their mother met the school's reading teacher, who set up short daily sessions with coloured letter cards. Yash promised to stop teasing and sat with her during practice.
